deck.title: Reliable computational workflow through physics
deck.visual_contract: Each slide is a single ImageGen-generated raster image embedded full-slide.
deck.delivery_context: 120-minute Week 2 teaching deck; timing appears only in speaker notes and package metadata, never in student-facing slide content.
deck.branding_override: No branding, logo, watermark, URL, footer, or institutional mark is permitted.
deck.canvas: 16:9 pure white canvas; no outer border or frame; no mesh, network, molecular, corner, texture, gradient, or background decoration; locked Roboto Condensed Bold navy title and Roboto Medium charcoal subtitle at the same upper-left anchor on every slide

slides.title: Reliable computational workflow through physics
slides.subtitle: Week 2 | Functions, vectorisation, debugging, and testing
visual_text: An ideal oscillator is simple enough to know — and rich enough to expose weak computational reasoning.
Can readable code, independent tests, and physical evidence make a calculation trustworthy?
decompose | predict | implement | test | interpret

notes.checkpoint: Ask what evidence students would want before trusting an oscillator plot.
notes.transition: Frame MATLAB as the instrument used to expose the reasoning chain.

slides.title: Today’s arc: decompose → predict → implement → test
slides.subtitle: A compact physics model becomes a defensible computational result.
visual_text: 1 Physical question
2 Dependencies + pseudocode
3 Vectorised implementation
4 Layered tests
5 Debugging + practical transfer
Outcomes: preserve units, align arrays, classify defects, design tests, explain physical evidence

notes.checkpoint: Which step is missing when an AI assistant returns code immediately after the question?
notes.transition: Establish the standard of evidence before writing any syntax.

slides.title: A trustworthy program is an argument
slides.subtitle: Running code is only one claim in a longer chain.
visual_text: Physics question → model + assumptions → dependencies → algorithm → code → independent tests → physical interpretation
Each arrow is a decision that can be inspected.
A plausible graph is not yet evidence.

notes.checkpoint: Ask students to identify one claim that a successful Run button cannot verify.
notes.transition: Introduce a model whose expected behaviour is known before computation.

slides.title: Worked model: an ideal mass–spring oscillator
slides.subtitle: Known physics gives us strong reference behaviour.
visual_text: m d²x/dt² = −kx
x(t) = A cos(ωt + φ)
v(t) = −Aω sin(ωt + φ)
ω = √(k/m)    T = 2π/ω
Assumptions: linear spring, point mass, no damping, horizontal motion, equilibrium at x = 0

notes.checkpoint: Predict x, v, and the direction of motion at t = T/4.
notes.transition: Map every symbol to a readable variable and unit.

slides.title: Map symbols to names, meanings, and units
slides.subtitle: Readable names keep dimensions visible while the model becomes code.
visual_text: m → mass_kg → kg
k → springConstant_N_per_m → N/m
A → amplitude_m → m
ω → omega_rad_per_s → rad/s
t → t_s → s
x, v, E → x_m, v_m_per_s, totalEnergy_J
Dimensional check: k/m has units s⁻²; √(k/m) has units s⁻¹.

notes.checkpoint: Have students derive the unit of omega without using a memorised formula.
notes.transition: Separate inputs, derived quantities, outputs, and checks before coding.

slides.title: Decompose before writing MATLAB
slides.subtitle: A dependency map prevents important decisions from disappearing into syntax.
visual_text: Inputs: m, k, A, φ, final time, sampling resolution
Derived: ω = √(k/m), T = 2π/ω
Outputs: t, x(t), v(t), energy
Checks: units, initial values, bounds, repeat period, energy conservation
Question to ask: which quantities depend on which earlier decisions?

notes.checkpoint: Ask whether total energy is an input, a derived quantity, an output, or a check.
notes.transition: Turn the dependency map into structured pseudocode.

slides.title: Pseudocode is executable reasoning
slides.subtitle: It records the algorithm before MATLAB or AI chooses the syntax.
visual_text: 1 Define physical inputs with units
2 Compute ω and T
3 Create one aligned time array
4 Evaluate x, v, K, U, and E at every time
5 Apply independent checks
6 Interpret the motion and state limitations
Pseudocode should preserve dependencies and decisions — not imitate MATLAB punctuation.

notes.checkpoint: Ask students what must happen before the time array can be designed.
notes.transition: Implement the analytical model once for every time using arrays.

slides.title: Vectorisation evaluates one model across an array
slides.subtitle: The mathematics stays visible when array operations match the formula.
visual_text: omega_rad_per_s = sqrt(springConstant_N_per_m/mass_kg);
t_s = linspace(0,4*period_s,1001);
x_m = amplitude_m.*cos(omega_rad_per_s.*t_s + phase_rad);
v_m_per_s = -amplitude_m.*omega_rad_per_s.*sin(...);
kineticEnergy_J = 0.5.*mass_kg.*v_m_per_s.^2;
potentialEnergy_J = 0.5.*springConstant_N_per_m.*x_m.^2;
totalEnergy_J = kineticEnergy_J + potentialEnergy_J;
Element-wise operators preserve one result per stored time.

notes.checkpoint: Which operators need dots, and why does scalar multiplication not require one here?
notes.transition: Make the alignment expectation explicit as an array-shape contract.

slides.title: Shape contracts make array alignment testable
slides.subtitle: One time value must correspond to one position, velocity, and energy value.
visual_text: Contract: size(t_s) = size(x_m) = size(v_m_per_s) = size(totalEnergy_J)
Aligned arrays support plotting, indexing, and element-by-element comparisons.
Common defects: row versus column mismatch | unintended implicit expansion | wrong colon order
Check both shape and finiteness before interpreting values.
A scalar loop is a useful independent cross-check of a vectorised result.

notes.checkpoint: What plausible output might implicit expansion create when two vectors have different orientations?
notes.transition: Move from array correctness to a ladder of independently failing tests.

slides.title: Testing should climb from execution to physics
slides.subtitle: Different layers expose different classes of defect.
visual_text: 1 Runs without error — syntax only
2 Shapes align and values are finite
3 Known values match at t = 0
4 Physical bounds hold: |x| ≤ A
5 The state repeats after one period
6 An invariant holds: K + U is constant
7 A scalar implementation agrees with the vectorised one
No single layer proves the whole model.

notes.checkpoint: Which test can pass even if the physical formula contains the wrong sign?
notes.transition: Use exact states to build low-cost, interpretable tests.

slides.title: Known states give cheap, powerful checks
slides.subtitle: Evaluate behaviour where the physics already supplies an answer.
visual_text: At t = 0: x = A, v = 0
At t = T/4: x = 0, v = −Aω
At t = T/2: x = −A, v = 0
At t = T: x = A, v = 0
Use tolerances for floating-point comparisons; do not demand exact equality blindly.
A test is useful when its failure points toward a specific cause.

notes.checkpoint: Ask students to predict the velocity sign at one quarter-period before revealing it.
notes.transition: Add a physical invariant that checks the entire time history.

slides.title: Energy conservation checks the whole trajectory
slides.subtitle: An ideal undamped oscillator exchanges kinetic and potential energy.
visual_text: K(t) = ½mv²    U(t) = ½kx²
E(t) = K + U = ½kA² = 0.0576 J
At maximum displacement: U is maximum, K = 0
At equilibrium: K is maximum, U = 0
The total should remain constant across every stored time.
An invariant is strong evidence — but it still has a blind spot.

notes.checkpoint: Ask what the energy curves should look like before running the lecture demonstration.
notes.transition: Reveal a wrong velocity formula that still passes the energy test.

slides.title: One passing test is evidence — not proof
slides.subtitle: A wrong velocity sign still preserves total energy because velocity is squared.
visual_text: Correct: v(t) = −Aω sin(ωt + φ)
Defect:  v_wrong(t) = +Aω sin(ωt + φ)
Energy test: PASS — both velocities produce the same v²
Quarter-period sign test: FAIL — the mass moves in the wrong direction
Design tests that fail independently and expose different assumptions.
A conserved scalar may hide a wrong phase or direction.

notes.checkpoint: Ask students why the energy invariant cannot see the sign defect.
notes.transition: Generalise the diagnosis into a controlled debugging cycle.

slides.title: Debugging is another controlled experiment
slides.subtitle: Change one suspected cause and preserve the evidence.
visual_text: 1 Reproduce from a clean run
2 Localise the first doubtful quantity
3 State one hypothesis about the cause
4 Design the smallest discriminating test
5 Repair one cause
6 Rerun all previous tests
7 Explain the physical consequence
Avoid random edits: every change should answer a hypothesis.

notes.checkpoint: Ask what evidence should be recorded before editing the code.
notes.transition: Use categories to choose tests for plausible candidate code.

slides.title: Diagnose plausible code by defect category
slides.subtitle: Different defects require different evidence.
visual_text: Formula defect: omega = sqrt(k*m) → check units and period scale
Logical defect: 0:tMax:dt → inspect endpoints and number of values
Array defect: x^2 → inspect shapes; use element-wise powers for vectors
Communication defect: plot(v,x) → compare axes with the claimed graph
Numerical defect: exact equality → repeat with a physically justified tolerance
For each: category | consequence | correction | test that would fail

notes.checkpoint: Give one candidate line at a time and ask for the first discriminating test, not merely the correction.
notes.transition: Show how readable structure makes the same diagnosis faster.

slides.title: Readable code exposes the scientific structure
slides.subtitle: Compact code is not automatically clearer, faster, or more trustworthy.
visual_text: Readable workflow
Named inputs with units
Derived quantities computed once
Aligned arrays
Checks beside the claim they support
Interpretation in physical language
Opaque workflow
Magic numbers | compressed expressions | unlabeled plots | hidden workspace state
Optimise for auditability before cleverness.

notes.checkpoint: Ask which naming choice would help a classmate catch a unit mismatch.
notes.transition: Apply the same standard when an AI assistant proposes code.

slides.title: Use AI as a critic and pair programmer — not an authority
slides.subtitle: The student remains responsible for the model, decisions, and validation evidence.
visual_text: Before AI: predict behaviour, define units, decompose the problem, write pseudocode
With AI: ask for alternatives, explanations, edge cases, and tests
After AI: inspect every dependency, run independent checks, modify deliberately, interpret physically
Record what was accepted, changed, or rejected — and why.
A confident explanation from AI is not validation evidence.

notes.checkpoint: Ask for one prompt that makes Copilot critique code rather than merely generate it.
notes.transition: Transfer the workflow to the practical's projectile model.

slides.title: Practical bridge: debug and validate a projectile model
slides.subtitle: Start individually; then make every group claim answerable with evidence.
visual_text: 1 Complete the Week 02 Individual Practical Check — Quiz in Google Classroom
2 Predict the trajectory and write pseudocode before using AI
3 Build aligned x(t) and y(t) arrays
4 Diagnose a plausible defective candidate
5 Validate initial state, horizontal velocity, peak, range, and ground condition
6 Declare AI use and the decisions your group retained
Transfer question: which oscillator checks have a projectile analogue?

notes.checkpoint: Collect one proposed projectile check from each part of the room.
notes.transition: End the lecture and direct students to the Week 02 Individual Practical Check — Quiz in Google Classroom before group work begins.
